body:
There are a few things in life Donald Trump simply cannot stand. Among them:
Fake news
Low-energy people
Bad deals
Losing (Not allowed)
Rosie O’Donnell
But there’s one thing he probably hates even more than “fat pigs” with TDS: endless wars.
In some alternate universe, Trump gets glowing profiles in the New York Times for trying to unwind global conflicts instead of managing them forever. We do not live in that universe. 
While the MSM shies away from pointing this out, he’s been mostly consistent on this for years. The Iraq War? A mess. Nation-building? Waste of time. The basic philosophy is simple: If you’re going to fight, win. If not, get out.
Now, let’s be clear: Trump is no isolationist or pacifist. If Qasem Soleimani were still around, he could personally confirm Trump is not afraid to press the button. He’s perfectly comfortable using force.
 
What he doesn’t like is getting stuck.
Another thing Trump hates: Being played.
He sees himself as the ultimate dealmaker. So, when world leaders turn negotiations into theater, dragging things out, moving goalposts, giving history lectures mid-meeting, especially when he’s been nice to said leader (ahem…Putin), that’s when the temperature rises.
We literally saw this in Alaska:
Red carpet
B-2 bomber overhead
Whole “let’s end a war” setup
And… no deal.
That’s basically Trump’s nightmare scenario: maximum buildup, zero deal.
Now fast forward to Iran.
Despite a large pile of Iranian mullahs learning the hard way that the afterlife may not come with the amenities they were promised… The regime still seems bent on arranging a meeting with a bunker buster.
That’s a problem for for the mullahs, but it’s also a problem for Trump. Because the longer this drags on:
Gas prices creep up
Negative headlines stack up
Approval starts drifting down
And Trump hates 
all three of those things.
So what’s the play?
If you take Trump at his word, and more importantly, his pattern… he’s going to push hard to end this quickly (ideally without ending a civilization.)
But here’s the twist:
That doesn’t necessarily mean a clean, signed, “Mission Accomplished” deal. It could just as easily end the way a lot of these things do: not with a signature… but with everyone slowly backing away from the table and pretending it’s over.
That’s what makes the Iran deal market interesting right now. There are obviously more important issues at hand with Iran than prediction markets. But, understanding how all of this ends is vital to inform the future of our economy, our politics, and our sanity. You might think the conflict is going to end, be completely right, and yet still take a bath on your market position because no one officially “agreed to, signed, or accepted a new Iran-US nuclear deal” as the rules on this market state. Take a look at the current numbers from Polymarket:
At the time of publication, each market was below 50%.
Before April: 10%
Before May: 25%
Before June: 44%
Which tells you the market sees:
Pressure to resolve this
But very low confidence in a clean, formal deal
If Trump’s core instinct holds (no quagmires, no drawn-out messes) then 
some form of resolution
 feels more likely than not. But the key distinction is this:
The market is pricing a 
deal.

Trump may be aiming for an 
ending.
And those are not always the same thing.
